You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Market sentiment shifts sharply: Oil prices fall, tech stocks rise, yen nears intervention threshold—global markets enter a crucial week

TEXT:
At the start of the new week, U.S. stock index futures indicate that technology stocks are likely to rebound mildly. This week, Korea’s memory chip giants will once again test the resilience of artificial intelligence trading. Potential increases in energy supply are pushing oil prices lower, which could ease inflationary pressures; meanwhile, investors are awaiting the arrival of key earnings season for the AI sector.
Most European stock indexes opened higher, with momentum in semiconductor stocks weakening, but other sectors rising. The European Stoxx 600 index hovers near record highs. London’s FTSE 100 rose 0.1%, the Paris CAC 40 rose 0.2%, Germany’s DAX was unchanged, and performance among tech companies diverged. Italy’s FTSE MIB rose 0.4%. Spain’s IBEX 35 fell 0.3%.
As investors return to markets after the Independence Day holiday, U.S. stocks appear set to catch up on the gains missed last Friday. Nasdaq 100 futures rose 1%, S&P 500 futures up 0.4%, and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures up 0.1%.
Asian stocks fluctuated; South Korea’s hot stock market cooled slightly last week but is still up 90% year-to-date as AI demand and tight supply pushed chip prices higher. On Monday, Korea’s KOSPI fell 0.5%, while Japan’s Nikkei was flat.
Last week, the U.S. benchmark stock index rose 1.8%, while the European STOXX index was up 2.7%. With energy prices cooling, traders trimmed rate hike bets, though some areas of the tech sector—especially chip manufacturing —remained under pressure.
Focus on Sector Rotation
Against a backdrop of a quiet economic data calendar and U.S. earnings season yet to fully kick off, these events have gained importance. Meanwhile, recent global market performance has been mixed, and investors are starting to question whether the AI-driven rally over the past quarter has gone too far.
Singular Bank strategy head Roberto Scholtes said: "Speculative positions in semiconductors and other popular tech themes may continue to be pared back. The key question is whether this will trigger a rotation into lagging sectors or prompt a broader correction."
Global chip stock volatility is currently at its highest since 2020
(Source: Bloomberg )
Semiconductor Stock Momentum is Weakening
So far this year, chip manufacturers have led the AI rally. Morgan Stanley strategists say that as investors withdraw from some of this year's largest tech trades, U.S. equities may find it difficult to hit new highs. The team led by Michael Wilson noted that, as investors shift towards lagging sectors including AI hyperscalers, semiconductor momentum is dissipating.
Francisco Simon, head of Europe strategy at Santander Asset Management, said: "The upcoming earnings season may be necessary to rebuild market confidence in this field. That said, the medium-term trend remains intact."
Jefferies’ chief European economist Mohit Kumar said: "Oil price declines should support growth-sensitive sectors and countries that have trailed over the past three months."
He noted: "While we remain bullish on U.S. tech, we have increased our holdings in Asian markets and growth-sensitive sectors in recent weeks."
Earnings Season Highlights Ahead
As earnings season approaches, investors will closely watch the performance of artificial intelligence-related companies, particularly as the market worries about an AI bubble.
This week, notable U.S. earnings include Delta Air Lines and PepsiCo. However, Samsung Electronics will be in the spotlight on Tuesday, when the chipmaker will be scrutinized by the market—analysts expect its profit to be up 18-fold. The stock is up 165% year-to-date. A few days later, SK Hynix will conduct a $29 billion U.S. public listing.
According to regulatory filings, Korean chipmaker SK Hynix will begin its U.S. IPO on Monday, aiming to raise about $28 billion. This will further test the strength of the AI wave.
Hormuz Strait Transport Flows Continue to Recover
Oil prices fell as shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz continued to recover, and OPEC+ signaled increased supply. Brent crude dropped about 0.7% to $71.65 per barrel.
Despite a lack of progress in the fractious U.S.-Iran peace talks, vessels continue to pass through the Hormuz Strait. Last week, from Monday to Saturday, 160 vessels passed through. Meanwhile, OPEC+ agreed to raise production targets by a further 188,000 barrels per day starting August.
Soojin Kim at Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group said: "Brent and Dubai crude oil futures remain in contango, reflecting ample near-term supply; Gulf energy producers are expected to further cut official selling prices to maintain competitiveness."
Contango means front-month futures prices are lower than forward contract prices. Analysts say Saudi exports have rebounded sharply, close to prewar levels, and the UAE is quickly restoring flows, making the physical market more relaxed.
